articles.title: Give parallel browser jobs an account-level budget
articles.excerpt: A team splits a monthly reporting task across four browser sessions. Each session navigates independently. All four use the same account, request exports at once, and reach the same account-level limi…
articles.body: A team splits a monthly reporting task across four browser sessions. Each session navigates independently. All four use the same account, request exports at once, and reach the same account-level limit. The navigation is isolated. The workload still needs coordination. This is a design walkthrough for that problem, not a measurement of a particular portal or a claim about BrowserAct throughput. BrowserAct supports parallel sessions that share a browser's login state while keeping their active navigation separate. That capability answers where a task runs. Your application still needs to decide when a shared account should receive more work.

articles.title: AWS Web Answer Turns One MCP Call Into a Cited Answer — Here's What It Costs and Where It Stops
articles.excerpt: If you have ever built the "answer a question from the web" pipeline for an agent, you know the shape of it: search API, fetch pages, chunk, retrieve, synthesize, then bolt citations on at the end and…
articles.body: If you have ever built the "answer a question from the web" pipeline for an agent, you know the shape of it: search API, fetch pages, chunk, retrieve, synthesize, then bolt citations on at the end and hope they point at real sources. On 5 November 2026, AWS made that whole pipeline a single tool call — Web Answer is now generally available on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. One MCP tool call. A natural-language question goes in, a synthesized answer comes back, with citations attached. That is the whole pitch, and it is a genuinely useful one. But the price, the region limit and the rate limit decide whether it fits your agent, so this article will keep the pitch and the price tag separate. What actually shipped Web Answer is a managed connector in AgentCore Gateway.

articles.body: A nightly job that rewrites 412 support tickets into short summaries used to run on my laptop, and that was fine until I wanted my laptop back at night. So I moved the batch onto a free server, kept the model calls on free model access, and gave myself 48 hours to decide whether I trusted it. The first full run finished in 31 minutes with exit code 0 and a tidy log line, and nine of the 412 inputs had never been touched at all. Isn't a green build that quietly drops records the worst possible outcome for a batch job? Disclosure: This article was prepared as part of MonkeyCode's product outreach.

articles.title: DSCR for a Rental Loan File: Rent PITIA, With the Formula Shown
articles.excerpt: By Brandon Sooknanan, Founder of StatementReady On a DSCR loan file, the property's rent is compared to its housing payment instead of using the borrower's personal income from bank statements. Lender…
articles.body: By Brandon Sooknanan, Founder of StatementReady On a DSCR loan file, the property's rent is compared to its housing payment instead of using the borrower's personal income from bank statements. Lender definitions of rent and of what counts in the payment can vary, so treat published matrices as background and the lender's own matrix as the rule for the file you are building. The formula DSCR = monthly gross rent ÷ monthly PITIA, rounded to two decimals. If you turn on an optional vacancy or expense factor, rent is first multiplied by (100% − the factor you enter). The free calculator sets no factor and no minimum ratio.

articles.title: Same Model Name, Different Answers: A Drift Probe for Free Model Endpoints
articles.excerpt: My eval suite passed on Monday. On Friday the same inputs failed. Nothing in my repo changed. So what changed? The endpoint behind the model name. I have been running small workloads against free mode…
articles.body: My eval suite passed on Monday. On Friday the same inputs failed. Nothing in my repo changed. So what changed? The endpoint behind the model name. I have been running small workloads against free model access, with the probe job itself living on a free server. This post is the FAQ I wish I had read first. It is a myth-busting list, and each myth comes with a check you can run yourself. Why does the same request return different answers a week later? Because a model name is a routing label, not a checksum. Providers patch weights, swap quantizations, and move traffic between backends. Your config file never hears about it. You cannot prevent that. You can only notice it early, on your schedule instead of your users' schedule. That is what the artifact below does.

articles.title: What's that bright 'star' in the early morning sky? It's not a star at all!
articles.excerpt: Spotted a dazzling light in the eastern sky before sunrise? It's Venus, and the planet is only going to get brighter as it heads toward its spectacular peak later this month.
articles.body: Early morning risers heading to work or school before sunrise are likely to notice a very bright, star-like object appearing low in the east-southeast sky just before sunrise. What is somewhat amazing is that just a couple of weeks ago this object wasn't there at all, but now it literally stands out with such brilliance as to almost command the attention of commuters who might be traveling in an easterly direction to "Look at me!" The object in question is, of course, the planet Venus, which is currently amid one of its most spectacular forays into the morning sky, literally "vaulting up" into prominence. On Oct. 24, Venus came to inferior conjunction, passing between the Earth and sun and shifting from the evening into the morning sky.

articles.title: You can see another galaxy with the naked eye — here's how to find it
articles.excerpt: The Andromeda galaxy is one of the most distant things you can see with the naked eye. The difficult part isn't finding it. It's believing that faint smudge really is another galaxy.
articles.body: The first time I showed someone the Andromeda galaxy (M31), our conversation did not go quite as planned. I'd carefully worked my way across the sky, starting from the Great Square of Pegasus and hopping from star to star until I was confident I had the right patch. I pointed the telescope, got M31 in its crosshairs and proudly announced to my wife that I had found the closest giant galaxy to the Milky Way . Would she like to see it? She then stayed quiet for a little too long as she looked through the eyepiece. Then came an unexpected question. "Is it near that little smudge?" Hmmm. "Err, no. It is that little smudge," I replied. There was a pause. Of course, I knew exactly what had happened.

articles.title: Giant exoplanet emerges from the dark when the James Webb Space Telescope turns out the starlight
articles.excerpt: Astronomers have filtered out starlight from James Webb Space Telescope observations to see a giant exoplanet emerge in the darkness.
articles.body: Sometimes science can seem really counter-intuitive. For example, occasionally in astronomy, you can see more with less light. Case in point: the emergence of a giant planet in observations made by the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST), when astronomers found a way to block out light from the planet's parent star. The extrasolar planet, or exoplanet , in question is 51 Eridani b (51 ERI b), a gas giant with the same mass as around 11 Jupiters that orbits a star located around 97 light-years away. 51 ERI b was discovered back in 2015 by ground-based telescopes, but the planet was missing from observations of the system made by the JWST.

articles.body: ESA/Hubble & NASA, M. Libralato, G. Piotto, A. Sarajedini This NASA/ESA Hubble Space Telescope image released Nov. 5, 2026, provides a lesson in galactic history. The sparkling collection of stars is named Messier 30 (M30) after the French astronomer, Charles Messier , who cataloged M30 and other diffuse objects that might be mistaken for comets in the early telescopes of Messier’s time.
